target.title: feat(browser): pair the Chrome extension directly to a remote gateway
target.body:
Related: #53599

## What Problem This Solves

When Chrome runs on a different machine than the Gateway (the common managed-hosting shape: Gateway on a VPS, your signed-in Chrome on your laptop), there was no way to share that browser with an agent through the extension. The extension relay only listened on the Gateway host's loopback, so pairing a laptop Chrome required installing an OpenClaw node host on the laptop just to bridge the socket. This is the cross-machine gap called out in #53599: the old cross-machine relay was removed, and the restored extension (#100619) only covered same-host and node-host topologies.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds the **direct extension to Gateway** topology so the browser machine needs nothing but the Chrome extension: no OpenClaw install, Node, CLI, or open inbound port. The Gateway exposes a `/browser/extension` WebSocket route; the extension connects straight to it over `wss://`.

Key design decision: the route is registered with `auth: "plugin"` and no `nodeCapability`, so the Gateway does **not** pre-enforce its token auth. This is deliberate: browser WebSockets cannot set an `Authorization` header, so the handler instead self-validates the same host-local relay secret (hashed, constant-time compare) carried in the pairing string's `?token=`, exactly like a signed webhook. It also origin-checks `chrome-extension://` and resolves the extension profile before attaching the socket to the **same** `ExtensionRelayBridge` the loopback relay already uses, so all CDP synthesis, the OpenClaw tab-group consent boundary, and the in-process Playwright `/cdp` client are unchanged. The pairing path ends in `/extension`, so the extension's existing pairing parser accepts a `wss://gateway/browser/extension#<secret>` string with **zero extension code changes**.

Non-goals: this does not change the same-host or node-host paths, add any new config/env surface, or alter the loopback relay's auth.

## User Impact

Operators running a remote Gateway can now share a laptop's signed-in Chrome with an agent by installing only the extension:

```bash
# on the Gateway:
openclaw browser extension pair --gateway-url wss://your-gateway.example.com
# -> prints wss://your-gateway.example.com/browser/extension#<secret>
# load + pair the extension on the laptop; it connects straight to the Gateway.
```

No node host, no inbound port on the laptop. Serve the Gateway over TLS (`wss://`) so the pairing secret and CDP traffic are encrypted. Same-host and node-host pairing are unchanged.

## Evidence

- **Full validation (Blacksmith Testbox, rebased on latest `main`):** `tsgo:extensions` + `tsgo:extensions:test` clean (exit 0), `lint:extensions` clean, full browser suite **1485 passed | 1 skipped**.
- **Unit tests (run in CI):** 6 new tests in `gateway-relay-route.test.ts` cover the handler's branches: non-relay path returns `false` (Gateway continues), `503` when the control service is down, `403` on a non-`chrome-extension://` origin, `404` for a non-extension profile, `401` on a bad/absent secret, and successful `attach` on a valid secret.
- **Live proof of the relay loop:** a real headed Chrome for Testing loading the built extension paired over the `/browser/extension` route, `chrome.debugger` attached with **no** remote-debugging prompt, and CDP drove a real tab in the orange OpenClaw tab group (`Runtime.evaluate` round-tripped page content; screenshot captured). This reuses the same extension to bridge to CDP to Chrome path proven end-to-end in #100619.
- **Gateway dispatch verified against core source** (the real-Gateway upgrade seam): for an unprotected `auth:"plugin"` route with no `nodeCapability`, `server-http.ts` computes `shouldEnforceDefaultPluginGatewayAuth` = false (`PROTECTED_PLUGIN_ROUTE_PREFIXES` is only `["/api/channels"]`), skips gateway token auth, and calls `handlePluginUpgrade`, where `matchedPluginRoutesRequireGatewayAuth` = false and `getMissingPluginRouteRuntimeContext` = undefined, so it invokes the plugin route's `handleUpgrade`. That is the exact seam this handler relies on (`src/gateway/server-http.ts`, `src/gateway/server/plugins-http.ts`, `src/gateway/server/plugins-http/route-auth.ts`).
- **Docs:** `docs/tools/chrome-extension.md` now documents all three topologies (same host / direct-to-Gateway / via node host) and the per-host secret model.
